children.h: 1 · Is the infant sick or bleeding?

children.cond: High-pitched cry, arching, abnormal tone or poor suck in a deeply jaundiced infant

pill.text: Emergency department now: possible bilirubin encephalopathy — total and direct bilirubin and albumin now; intensive phototherapy now; neonatal team for urgent exchange transfusion; sepsis evaluation

children.cond: Poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, fever or low temperature, poor color

pill.text: Emergency department now: blood and urine culture, urine reducing substances, glucose, INR; neonatal or pediatric ICU if unstable

children.cond: Vomiting on milk feeds, E. coli or other gram-negative sepsis, cataracts — galactosemia possible, newborn screen pending or missing

pill.text: Send urine reducing substances now, before the switch; then stop breast milk and lactose formula — feed a soy-based or elemental formula and keep feeding; check glucose. Red-cell GALT activity (false-normal after transfusion). Mother expresses milk to keep her supply (lesson 02-03)

children.cond: Bleeding — umbilical stump, bruising, blood in stool or vomit, bulging fontanelle

pill.text: Emergency department now: vitamin K IV (slowly) now, INR, head imaging if neurologic signs — vitamin K deficiency bleeding until proved otherwise. Ask whether vitamin K was given at birth

children.text: Still jaundiced at 2 weeks or later — breastfed or formula-fed — measure total and direct (or conjugated) bilirubin today. Do not wait for 3–4 weeks.
Preterm or on parenteral nutrition: same rule. Biliary atresia hides among sick and PN-fed infants.
You cannot see the fraction: about 1 in 3 breastfed infants still look yellow at 3 weeks (Maisels 2014).
Look at the stool yourself, and use a stool color card. Pale stools can come and go.

children.cond: Pale, clay-colored or white stools, or dark urine that stains the diaper — whatever the numbers

pill.text: Same-day pediatric hepatology: fractionated bilirubin and INR today — biliary atresia until proved otherwise. Look at the stool yourself

children.text: Read the direct or conjugated value itself, never the ratio. A hemolyzed sample lowers the direct value — redraw rather than reassure.

children.cond: Direct or conjugated ≥ 1.0 mg/dL (17 µmol/L), at any total

pill.text: Cholestasis: call pediatric GI or hepatology today — same-day visit if stools are pale or the value is rising. Urinalysis and urine culture. INR — if prolonged, parenteral vitamin K and recheck INR. Do not wait for an ultrasound

children.cond: Above the lab's upper limit but below 1.0 mg/dL

pill.text: Not normal: discuss with pediatric hepatology today and repeat within days (expert opinion)

children.text: Review the newborn screen (hypothyroidism, galactosemia) and check TSH and free T4 (AAP 2022).
Weight trajectory and feeding. CBC with reticulocytes and DAT if pale, or if jaundice is deepening.

children.cond: Hemolysis, high TSH or low free T4, poor weight gain, formula-fed, bilirubin rising, or still jaundiced at 3 months (expert opinion)
children.subtext: Work up the cause; hepatology clinic for persistent jaundice

children.cond: Thriving breastfed infant, normal exam, pigmented stools, conjugated value normal

pill.text: Likely breast-milk jaundice: keep breastfeeding. Still jaundiced → recheck total and direct bilirubin in 2–4 weeks (expert opinion). Pale stool or dark urine → same day
